description:
Rosebital is the technology team of Gulizar Zeki Obdan Anadolu Lisesi in Istanbul, Türkiye. 

Our name combines “rose” and “orbital”, inspired by the rose gardens that give our school its name. We imagine roses blooming in orbits out in space.

We are a team of high school students who love software, 3D modeling and design, and this is our first NASA Space Apps Challenge. We want to learn, build something real, and tell a story about space exploration using NASA data.
summary:
The Last Signal is an interactive digital museum for space enthusiasts: a museum of exhibits that can never be displayed on Earth. 

Its exhibits are the spacecrafts humanity left behind on Mars, Moon and the Space. Since they cannot be brought home, the museum takes visitors to them. On a 3D globe built from NASA's Viking colour mosaic, glowing beacons mark where Opportunity, Spirit, Sojourner, Ingenuity, Viking 1 and 2, InSight, Surveyor 3 and Apollo 11, 12 and 15. Each beacon opens an exhibit: a three-picture story with NASA imagery, a label card with landing coordinates linked to their NASA sources, and a longer story written by our team. 

For several missions, visitors live the final moments of the crafts themselves: driving Opportunity into the 2018 dust storm, flying Ingenuity's last flight, trying to free Spirit from the sand. Every journey ends the way the real mission ended, because each exhibit tells of a "last signal". 

The museum turns "discarded equipment" into stories of endurance, so that enthusiasts see these silent machines as explorers that went far beyond what was planned.
details:
What it does
The Last Signal is an interactive digital museum: a museum of exhibits that can never be displayed on Earth. Its exhibits are the spacecraft humanity left behind on Mars and the Moon. Each one goes silent after sending its last signal home, and each one is still where it stopped. They can never come back, so the museum brings visitors to them.

The museum has two halls, Mars and the Moon. Visitors spin a 3D globe and find glowing beacons:

The Last Signal Mars view: Opportunity, Spirit, Sojourner, Ingenuity, Viking 1, Viking 2 and InSight

  • The Last Signal Moon view:  Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12 (one shared beacon, 180 m apart), Apollo 11 and Apollo 15

Every exhibit opens like a interactive museum display:

  • a three-picture story with original NASA images: the beginning, the big discovery, and the goodbye
  • a label card with key dates and landing coordinates, each linked to the NASA page it comes from
  • a longer story written by our team, ending with a short closing line

Interactive rooms
For several missions, visitors do not only read the story; they live the final moments of the spacecrafts:

  • driving Opportunity as the 2018 dust storm darkens the sky
  • flying Ingenuity's 72nd and last flight
  • trying to free Spirit from the sand before its last Martian winter

How it works
The museum runs entirely in the browser: HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules, with Three.js for 3D. There is no build step and no server code, so it opens on any laptop or phone.

  • Mars hall: NASA's Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic, taken from NASA Mars Trek.
  • Interactive rooms: our team sculpted the 3D ground, and we wrote a small tool that "bakes" it into light height maps and textures, so the rooms load quickly.
  • Languages: English and Turkish, switchable at any time.
  • Controls: keyboard, mouse and touch.

Benefits and intended impact
Most people know the famous launches, but few know how these machines' stories ended. Many worked far longer than planned: Opportunity was built for 90 days and lasted more than 14 years, and Sojourner was planned for 7 days and worked for 83. The Last Signal gives these "discarded" machines a place to be remembered, a museum they could never otherwise have. We want visitors to leave seeing them not as space junk but as explorers with a story of endurance, curiosity and goodbye.

What makes it creative

  • A museum for exhibits that cannot be displayed: instead of bringing objects to visitors, it brings visitors to the objects, on another world.
  • Endings that never change: however well you drive or fly, Opportunity's battery still runs out and Ingenuity's blade still breaks. Your choices change the numbers, not the result. Visitors live the real ending instead of "winning" it, so each game becomes a moment of empathy, not a score.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: every date, number and coordinate was checked against NASA, JPL and NSSDCA pages. Where our team's notes disagreed with a source, we used the source and recorded the difference in our README.
  • Clear language: short sentences and everyday words, so the stories work for visitors of any age.
  • Reach: runs on phones and low-power computers, with no install and no account.
  • Honest credits: every image, model, font and data source is listed with its licence. Our use of SI tools is declared in the README.

Tools

  • Software: Three.js, HTML/CSS/JavaScript (ES modules), Node.js (terrain baking tool), Python (local test server)
  • Data: NASA Mars Trek, NASA Photojournal, NASA Image and Video Library, NSSDCA
  • SI: Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code for software development, translation and fact-checking support; Claude Design for the logo; CapCut AI voice for the demo narration
  • Hardware: none; it runs in a web browser
